query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion in high‐entropy alloys is governed by a microstructurally driven mechanism in which controlled alloying (e.g., trace boron addition) refines the grain structure and promotes a uniform dispersion of hard second phases (such as in situ formed TiB2). This refined architecture facilitates the rapid formation and self‐renewal of a protective passive oxide film during wear, so that any mechanically induced damage is quickly re‐passivated, thereby inhibiting both mechanical degradation and localized corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., produced by laser cladding) exhibiting a mixed BCC and σ phase microstructure with moderate grain size and no targeted microalloying.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled amount of boron to promote the in situ formation of TiB2—for example, preparing coatings with an optimal B content (e.g., x = 0.5–1.0) to achieve grain refinement and second-phase dispersion.
generation.conditions: Perform tribocorrosion tests in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under defined sliding contact loads, alongside parallel tests in an inert atmosphere (e.g., UHV) to decouple the effects of oxygen-driven passivation.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain refinement and a homogeneous dispersion of hard second phases (e.g., TiB2 particles) that support the formation and sustaining of a dense, self-healing passive oxide film.
generation.mechanism: Under combined mechanical and corrosive stresses, the refined microstructure minimizes plastic deformation while promoting rapid re-passivation. The hard second phases act as both mechanical barriers and nucleation sites for the oxide film. As wear-generated damage occurs, a stable passive film is quickly restored, which limits both the mechanical removal of material and the initiation/progression of corrosion pits.
generation.predicted_outcome: The boron-modified, refined HEA is predicted to show significantly lower overall degradation in tribocorrosion tests—a reduction in both wear rate and corrosion current density, as well as smaller fluctuations in open circuit potential (ΔOCP) compared to a matched baseline without boron. In environments with oxygen (allowing for passive film formation), the synergistic protection will be evident, whereas in inert environments (where passivation is suppressed) the advantage will diminish.
generation.baseline: A comparable HEA coating prepared without boron addition, exhibiting a coarser microstructure and less uniform passive film formation under corrosive and mechanical stresses.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under conditions where oxygen is available to form and sustain a passive film and where mechanical loads are moderate enough to allow re-passivation. Under extreme inert conditions (e.g., ultrahigh vacuum) or when mechanical damage completely erodes the oxide layer before repassivation can occur, the protective mechanism may fail.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in the precise quantitative contributions of grain refinement versus second-phase dispersion to the rate of re-passivation and mechanical resistance. This proposal extends the findings reported in the laser-cladded AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx study (PMC12565319) and the inverse Hall-Petch behavior observed in polished HEA surfaces (PMC7311485) by integrating them into a unified model for tribocorrosion. The new aspect is the specific coupling of microstructural refinement with dynamic oxide film restoration under simultaneous wear and corrosion conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings on identical substrates: one with the optimal boron addition (yielding refined microstructure and dispersed TiB2) and one without boron (baseline coarse structure). Subject both sets to identical tribocorrosion tests in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under controlled sliding loads. Additionally, run parallel tests in an oxygen-deprived (inert) environment to isolate the effect of passive film formation.
measurements: Open circuit potential (OCP) tracking to measure ΔOCP during wear cycles
Corrosion current density from potentiodynamic polarization
Surface characterization (SEM/EDS) to evaluate oxide film formation and microstructural evolution pre- and post-test
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-modified, refined HEA does not exhibit significantly lower wear rates, reduced corrosion current densities, and more stable/passivating oxide films compared to the baseline under corrosive conditions—or if no difference is observed when oxygen is present to enable passivation—then the hypothesis that microstructural refinement coupled with dynamic passivation governs simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. This work studied an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy that was manufactured using a laser-based consolidation additive manufacturing process. We showed that low friction and high wear resistance are achievable with bare high entropy alloys in inert environments. These characteristics are linked to the shear-induced formation of a highly refined, near-amorphous surface film that exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior. The detrimental role of environments, specifically those that result in oxidation, was mitigated by tribological testing in a UHV environment. A newly proposed amorphization model was used to accurately predict the grain size-dependent shear strength, and thus friction coefficient.
